Its high-speed read/write performance is specifically tailored for video editors and VFX professionals.  Frontline video production teams are sometimes at risk of project interruptions due to unexpected SSD failures in storage devices. The TBS-h574TX supports hot-swappable SSDs, along with conditional automatic RAID replacement with spares. If an SSD enters a critical state, the system automatically moves data from the affected drive to a spare in the RAID group, seamlessly integrating it into the existing RAID without the need for RAID rebuilding. This significantly reduces the risk of data loss.

QNAP TBS-h574TX NASbook review: Fast workgroup storage | Macworld 
 When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence .

 At a glance
 Expert's Rating
 Pros
 Supports both M.2 and E.1S NVMe SSDs
 Excellent throughput via Ethernet (10Gbps) and Thunderbolt (20Gbps)
 Unique semi-retro look
 Myriad NAS/server software features
 Cons
 Not cheap. 
 Our Verdict 
 If you’re looking for fast, versatile workgroup storage, the highly capable TBS-h574TX deserves close scrutiny. It can be accessed directly via Thunderbolt or remotely via the network and offers all the software capabilities NAS/server boxes bring to the table.

 QNAP’s combo NAS/DAS (Network/Direct) attached TBS-h574TX storage box gives you the best of both worlds. It allows any number of users to connect to it over the local network at 10Gbps (or 2.5Gbps) and leverage it as shared storage or employ the myriad NAS/server apps and capabilities. But you can also attach it to your Mac’s Thunderbolt port for twice-as-fast 20Gbps (network bridge) local access to the data on board. Sweet.
 The TBS-h574TX is a somewhat retro-looking, squat rectangle of a NAS (network-attached storage)/direct-attached box measuring 2.36 inches thick, 8.46 inches wide, by 7.83 inches deep. It’s a most substantial piece of metal-based kit, weighing in at just a hair under 5 pounds. With the no-slip feet, there’s little chance of knocking this puppy off the desk. Just the same, make sure all cables are secured at some point before they reach the box. I’ve seen more instances of tripping on wires, pulling hardware off its perch, than actual displacement of the equipment itself.
 There are five bays with easy-access drive trays on board that accept state-of-the-art E.1S (see the explanation below) or M.2 (4.5mm heatsinks or thinner) NVMe SSDs. You can access the bays/tray from the front of the TBS-h574TX after removing the locking, pop-off, top half of the front cover.
 The SSD slots are PCIe 3.0, though you may use PCIe 4.0 or 5.0 SSDs, which are, of course, backwards compatible. I recommend PCIe 4.0 as PCIe 3.0 SSDs are becoming pricey and hard to come by, and PCIe 5.0 is expensive overkill.
 The front of the QNAP TBS-h574TX with its cover off to expose the hot-swappable SSD bays. 
 Along with the convenient Type-C Thunderbolt port on the face are another 10Gbps Type-A port, quick copy and power buttons, as well as power and activity indicator lamps.
 The Thunderbolt port on the back is PC/Mac connect-only, so you can’t use external devices or peripherals with it. Also on the back are 2.5Gbe and 10Gbe ports, a 10Gbps Type-A USB and 5Gbps Type-A port, as well as HDMI output. Then of course, there’s the coax power port.
 The back of the TBS-h574TX with its Ethernet ports, USB ports and dual exhaust fans. 
 Note that you do not need to shut down the TBS-h574TX just to swap out a bad drive. If you use a suitable RAID mode (1, 1+0, 5, etc.) the array will remain available and rebuild in the background. Remember that when you configure the storage in any RAID-capable device.
 As a fully functional NAS box/server, the TBS-h574TX we tested sported a 4.5Ghz, Core i5-1340PE (12 cores, 16 threads) and 16GB of DRAM, plus 5GB of NAND for basic functionality before you install the full operating system. Note that this differed from the a 4.4GHz Core i5-1235U CPU listed on the product page.
 If you’re not familiar with NAS and wonder “Why a CPU?”… The TBS-h574TX’s capabilities go far beyond simple storage. QNAP’s full-on QuTS hero OS, née (QTS NAS OS) and apps let it serve as a multimedia server, multimedia playback unit (via HDMI), a backup engine, virtual machine and docker host, surveillance station, and a lot more.
 I’ve used QNAP NAS boxes for years, and the backup capabilities (both local and cloud) are outstanding. Note that surveillance requires purchasing more licenses if you have more than one IP cam.
 Just some of the apps available for the QuTS hero OS that runs the TBS-h574TX. 
 What are EDSFF and E.1S?
 EDSFF stands for Enterprise and Data center SSD Form Factor and covers several sizes of thermally enhanced designs. E.1S is the smallest, meant for SMB and end-user devices. E.1S is 33.5mm wide, 118.75mm long, and from 9mm to 25mm thick. The connector is the same M.2 you’ll find on consumer NVMe SSDs, hence the interchangeability.
 Better heat-shedding is the main thrust of EDSFF. That’s to handle the heavier loads that many enterprise storage devices experience, warding off any thermal throttling that might occur with less robust thermal designs.
 How much does the QNAP TBS-h574TX cost?
 The unpopulated (no SSDs) Core i5 version of the box that I tested runs a rather hefty $1,500 (£3,299 in the U.K.). There’s a Core i3 version available for $1,200. Those prices are considerably higher than the average consumer NAS box. QNAP itself markets 2-bay models for less than $200, and 5-bay (3.5-inch) models for less than $700 that offer the same OS and software, if not hardware features.
 However, given five E.1S-compatible SSD bays, Thunderbolt connectivity, and very powerful CPUs, we’re not sweating the TBS-h574TX’s cost. It’s worth it if you have the need. 
 Just remember that you’ll need to populate the box. With normal M.2 SSDs, that could be well under $1,000. E.1S could get very expensive–several thousand dollars expensive. In fact, the one 7.6TB Kioxia XD7P model we found at CDW was over $7000. CDW is a high-quality service, not a bargain basement outfit, but yowser!
 How fast is the QNAP TBS-h574TX?
 The TBS-h574TX is fast in both modes: roughly 10 gigabits/1GBps across the network (given 10Gbe) and 20 gigabits/2GBps using the Thunderbolt bridge. Think Gen 2 USB and Gen 2×2 USB.
 The TBS-h574TX connected via Thunderbolt. 
 I tested using a single 8TB WD 8100, but it’s easily capable of saturating the PCIe 3.0 bus as well as the Thunderbolt bridge and 10Gbe.
 Immediately below are the benchmark results using 10Gbe ethernet. BlackMagicDesign’s Disk Speed Test shows about what you’d expect from a 10Gbps protocol with networking overhead.
 ATTO showed even better 10Gbe numbers. More in line with what you’d see from direct connected USB Gen 2 10Gbps. Nice.
 I’m not sure why AmorphousDiskMark is so pessimistic about the TBS-h574TX’s write speed over ethernet. The other benchmarks and our real-life experience say it’s faster.
 While not the fastest 20Gbps numbers we’ve seen, those shown below certainly prove that the TBS-h574TX direct-attached using a Thunderbolt Ethernet bridge is a lot faster then over 10Gbe.
 ATTO rates the TBS-h574TX even faster than Disk Speed Test with larger transfers. Well over 2GBps. 
 Again, for some reason AmorphousDiskMark delivers far slower write numbers using ethernet protocols than the other benchmarks.
 The TBS-h574TX doesn’t generate a lot of heat the way many Thunderbolt storage devices do. The case has a lot of surface area for shedding warmth, and the twin fans also (very quietly) remove a lot of it as well.
 As far as the performance of the HTML interface and the various functions such as backup, Docker, streaming etc. The relatively robust Intel CPU and 16GB of memory handle them quite nicely. I found all functions quite a bit sprightlier than with my older 253 series boxes. Not amazingly, but noticeably so.
 Should you buy the QNAP TBS-h574TX?
 The connective versatility of the TBS-h574TX makes it an excellent choice for artistic workgroups and creators. Share files over the network, use it directly attached for better performance, and leverage its numerous NAS/server features as needed. It’s business-grade equipment in a more prosumer-friendly form factor.
 That said, if you’re flying solo and don’t need to share content, straight Thunderbolt or USB4 storage will be both cheaper (not actually cheap…) and faster. You can then add NAS features with a cheaper box if needs be.

 How to Choose a NAS for Video Editing
 Buying a NAS for video editing isn’t just picking the biggest box on the shelf. The right answer depends on your codec, your team size, and whether you need to edit live from the network or work locally with proxies. Here’s the framework I walk every client through before they spend $1,000+ on hardware.
 Network Speed: 10GbE vs 2.5GbE vs Thunderbolt
 For 4K ProRes editing in 2026, 10GbE is the new baseline. A single 4K ProRes 422 HQ stream needs 250-500 MB/s sustained, which is more than 2.5GbE can deliver (around 295 MB/s real-world). 10GbE tops out near 1,180 MB/s, leaving room for multiple streams and headroom for color grading.
 Thunderbolt 4 direct attach (QNAP TBS-h574TX, UGREEN DXP8800 Plus) is the fastest option at up to 1.5 GB/s but only works for a single editor at a time without a Thunderbolt-aware switch. For multi-editor shops, 10GbE through a managed switch is still the most flexible choice.
 If you don’t edit uncompressed 4K and rely on H.264/H.265 with proxy workflows, 2.5GbE is honestly enough. The Synology DS425+ and DS925+ ship with dual 2.5GbE that will serve a solo creator perfectly.
 RAID Configuration for Video Projects
 RAID 5 gives you one-drive fault tolerance and the best capacity-to-cost ratio. RAID 6 (or SHR-2) survives two drive failures and is the right choice for any production environment where downtime costs real money. RAID 10 splits drives into mirrored pairs for the fastest random I/O, ideal for multicam timelines, at the cost of half your raw capacity.
 For an active 4-bay NAS like the DXP4800 Plus or DS925+, I run SHR-2/RAID 6 with three data drives plus one parity, accepting a 25% capacity penalty for two-drive safety. For an 8-bay like the DS1825+ or DXP8800 Plus, RAID 6 across six drives plus a hot spare is the production sweet spot.
 SSD Caching: When It Matters
 SSD caching speeds up random reads, which matters for multi-cam timelines and complex After Effects compositions with many small media files. For sequential 4K playback, spinning disks are already fast enough and caching won’t help. If your workload is heavy on random reads (Resolve color grading, large AE projects), add NVMe cache.
 Most modern NAS in this roundup support two M.2 NVMe slots for read or read-write cache. Plan to spend an extra $150-300 on a matched pair of NVMe drives; it transforms how the box feels under random I/O. Just remember Synology’s NVMe cache still requires Synology-branded drives, while UGREEN and QNAP accept standard retail NVMe.
 Drives, RAM, and Expansion
 For NAS drives in 2026, Seagate IronWolf and WD Red Plus remain the safe choices for most buyers. IronWolf Pro and WD Red Pro add longer warranties and higher workload ratings for busy NAS units. Avoid SMR drives (some older WD Blue models) at all costs; they choke on RAID rebuilds.
 RAM matters more than people think. 8GB is enough for file serving, but if you run Plex, Docker, or multiple apps, bump to 16GB minimum. The UGREEN DXP4800 Pro accepts up to 96GB, overkill for most but invaluable if you’re virtualizing.
 Plan expansion from day one. A 4-bay you think is enough today fills up fast once you start archiving client projects. Models with external expansion ports (Synology DX525, QNAP TL series) let you add drives without rebuilding your array.
 Budget Tier Recommendations
 Solo editor under $700: UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or Synology DS425+. Both deliver 4-bay RAID with 2.5GbE or 10GbE at reasonable cost. Pick the DXP4800 Plus if you want 10GbE today; pick the DS425+ if DSM’s software ecosystem matters more.
 Small team $700-$1,000: Synology DS925+ with a 10GbE add-in card, or stretch to the UGREEN DXP4800 Pro for virtualization headroom. Either handles 2-3 editors comfortably on 4K H.264/ProRes LT.
 Mid-size studio $1,000-$1,500: Synology DS1525+ or UGREEN DXP8800 Plus. Both have room to grow and enough horsepower for 5-10 editors on shared storage.
 Enterprise $1,500+: Synology DS1825+ with 25GbE networking or QNAP TBS-h574TX for Mac-based single-editor workflows. This tier handles uncompressed 4K and 6K with headroom.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What NAS speed do I need for 4K video editing?
 For 4K ProRes 422 HQ editing, plan on 250-500 MB/s of sustained throughput per stream. A 10GbE connection tops out around 1180 MB/s and comfortably handles multiple simultaneous 4K timelines. If you only edit H.264/H.265 with proxies, 2.5GbE (around 295 MB/s) is enough for a single editor.
 Is a NAS good for video editing?
 Yes. A modern NAS with 10GbE networking, an x86 CPU, and RAID 6 can absolutely serve video files to multiple editors simultaneously. For collaborative teams, a NAS is often more cost-effective than giving each editor their own SSD array. For solo editors, a NAS adds redundant backup and centralized project storage that local drives can’t match.
 Synology or QNAP for video editing?
 Synology wins on software polish (DSM is the most user-friendly NAS OS) and integration with backup, surveillance, and sync apps. QNAP wins on raw hardware variety, Thunderbolt NAS options, and faster CPUs at each price tier. For pure video editing, both work well; choose Synology if you value software maturity, QNAP if you need Thunderbolt or maximum hardware flexibility.
 Can I edit video directly from a NAS?
 Yes, provided your NAS has enough throughput for your codec. With 10GbE and a modern x86 NAS, ProRes 422, H.264, H.265, and BRAW all edit smoothly over the network. For uncompressed 4K or 6K, plan on 25GbE or Thunderbolt 4. If your network is only 1GbE, edit locally and use the NAS for archiving and backup.
 Final Verdict
 After 90 days of testing, the Synology DS1525+ remains our top pick for most video editing teams. Its 5-bay RAID 6 layout, 10GbE readiness, and best-in-class DSM software hit the sweet spot between price, performance, and reliability. If you need 8 bays for a growing team, step up to the Synology DS1825+. If budget matters most, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus gives you 10GbE speeds under $700, and the Synology DS925+ is the most hassle-free pick for a solo editor who wants the best NAS software on the market.
 Match your NAS to your codec and team size, not to marketing claims. For a single Mac editor, the QNAP TBS-h574TX Thunderbolt 4 NAS is a uniquely fast option. For 8-bay capacity on a budget, the UGREEN DXP8800 Plus punches well above its price. Whatever you pick, pair it with a UPS, run RAID 6 (or SHR-2), and back up to a second location. Your future self will thank you when a drive fails at 2 AM and your client deadline is at 9 AM.

UGREEN NAS Thunderbolt Direct-Attach Usage Guide

The Thunderbolt interface, co-developed by Intel and Apple, is a high-speed data transfer standard compatible with USB4 and USB3 devices. It not only delivers exceptional transfer speeds but also supports daisy-chaining multiple peripherals. Through Thunderbolt, users can achieve direct high-speed connections between computers and NAS devices for rapid data transfers.

Thunderbolt is renowned for its blazing-fast performance. The latest Thunderbolt 4 interface offers theoretical transfer speeds up to 40 Gbps (Thunderbolt 4 standard), far surpassing traditional interfaces. Whether transferring large files or processing real-time workloads, Thunderbolt significantly enhances productivity.

UGREEN NAS Thunderbolt Configuration Requirements

1. Supported NAS Models

The following UGREEN DXP series devices are equipped with Thunderbolt 4 ports and support Thunderbolt direct-attach functionality: DXP480T Plus, DXP6800 Pro, DXP8800 Series

2. Cable Requirements

Mandatory: Use Thunderbolt-certified cables (Thunderbolt 3/4/5) marked with the Thunderbolt symbol ⚡️.

Avoid: Generic USB-C cables (limited to USB protocols with ≤20 Gbps bandwidth).

3. Host Interface Requirements

Computer: Must have Thunderbolt 3 or newer ports (physical Type-C connector with Thunderbolt protocol support).

Notes:

● Although Type-C and Thunderbolt ports look identical, Thunderbolt uses a specialized communication protocol. Standard Type-C cables only support USB protocols and cannot deliver Thunderbolt’s high-speed data transfer capabilities. For optimal performance, use certified Thunderbolt cables.

● For Thunderbolt direct-attach connections, macOS is recommended due to higher transfer efficiency. Windows users must manually install drivers and address compatibility issues. Additionally, upload speeds may be slower on Windows systems.

Thunderbolt Direct-Attach Configuration Steps

1. Physical Connection:

Plug one end of the Thunderbolt cable into the Thunderbolt port on the UGREEN NAS, and the other end into the Thunderbolt port on your computer (Thunderbolt ports are typically marked with the ⚡️ symbol).

2. Device Recognition:

You can check the Thunderbolt connection status in either of the following ways:

Method 1: Automatic Recognition

After successful connection, the system will automatically assign a dedicated IP address to the Thunderbolt interface (e.g., 169.254.XX.XX).

● Path to Check: Go to [Control Panel > Network > Network Connection] and check the status of the "Thunderbolt" interface.

● Edit Network Settings (IPv4/IPv6): Click the "Edit" button. You can choose to obtain an IP address automatically (default) or manually configure an IP address and customize the MTU value.

Method 2: Client Auto-Search (Within LAN)

1. On the Thunderbolt-connected computer, open the UGREEN Cloud Client. On the local account login page, click "More Connections".

2. After login, use File Management to upload/download files and test the transfer speed of the Thunderbolt direct-attach connection.

Data Transfer Verification

You can validate the transfer speed of the Thunderbolt direct-attach connection using the following methods. This tutorial provides examples for both Windows and Mac systems.

Method 1: File Transfer via SMB

On a Windows computer:

1. Log in to your UGREEN NAS with an administrator account. Navigate to [Control Panel > File Service > SMB] and check the "Enable SMB Service" option. If this service is already enabled, skip this step.

2. In Windows, open "This PC" and click the "Map Network Drive" button.

3. In the "Folder" field, enter the \\Thunderbolt IP address of the NAS (e.g., \\169.254.12.125), then click "Browse" and double-click the NAS Thunderbolt IP address that appears.

4. Enter the NAS username and password to complete authentication, then establish the connection.

5. Select the NAS shared folder and mount it to the local computer. You can test the file transfer speed of the Thunderbolt direct-attach method by uploading/downloading files.

On a Mac book:

1. Log in to your UGREEN NAS with an administrator account. Navigate to [Control Panel > File Service > SMB] and check the "Enable SMB Service" option. If this service is already enabled, skip this step.

2. On a Mac computer, click [Finder > Go > Connect to Server].

3. Enter the NAS's Thunderbolt IP address (e.g., smb://169.254.4.109).

4. Enter the NAS username and password to connect.

5. Select the folder you want to access. After successful connection, you can test the transfer speed of the Thunderbolt direct-attach method by uploading/downloading files.

Note: Transfer speeds may differ between Windows and Mac systems. Typically, macOS achieves higher transfer speeds with Thunderbolt direct-attach compared to Windows.

Method 2: Transfer via Web Interface

1. On your local network, enter http://NAS_Thunderbolt_IP:9999 in a browser (e.g., http://169.254.4.109:9999) to log into the UGREEN NAS.

2. In the "Files", perform file upload/download operations to test the transfer speed of the Thunderbolt direct-attach method.

QNAP for creatives in 2026: Thunderbolt, ZFS, and the catch 
 Skip to content 
 QNAP is the one mainstream NAS brand that builds boxes specifically for editors: a Thunderbolt 4 port on the back, a real ZFS filesystem on the inside, and an HDMI-out so you can hang a monitor off it like a workstation. For a small post house deciding where the footage lives, that combination is rare and useful. The catch is not the hardware. It is the software surface that hardware drags along with it, and QNAP's security track record gives that surface more weight than it would on a simpler box. This is an honest guide to which QNAP makes sense for creative work in 2026, what QuTS hero ZFS buys you, and the part most reviews skip.
 The boxes built for editors # 
 QNAP shipped the world's first Thunderbolt 4 NAS in the TVS-h674T and TVS-h874T, and they remain the line's standout pitch for post in 2026. The 8-bay TVS-h874T runs a 12th-gen Intel Core i7 (12-core, 20-thread) or Core i9 (16-core, 24-thread), takes up to 64 GB of DDR4 ECC, holds eight SATA bays plus two M.2 2280 PCIe Gen 4 NVMe slots, and exposes two Thunderbolt 4 ports, two 2.5GbE ports, and an HDMI output (checked Jun 2026 against QNAP's spec sheet). The smaller TVS-h674T is the same idea in six bays on a Core i5-12400. Think of the Thunderbolt ports as a private express lane bolted onto a building that also has a normal front door: one editor can plug straight in at near-DAS speed while everyone else comes in over the network.
 QNAP's Thunderbolt 4 creator NAS, diskless, US pricing checked Jun 2026. Model CPU / RAM Bays + NVMe Direct + network Price (diskless) 
 TVS-h674T-i5-32G i5-12400 6-core / 32 GB 6 SATA + 2x M.2 Gen4 2x TB4, 2x 2.5GbE ~$2,500 
 TVS-h874T-i7-32G i7 12-core / 32 GB 8 SATA + 2x M.2 Gen4 2x TB4, 2x 2.5GbE $3,089 (QNAP store) 
 TVS-h874T-i9-64G i9 16-core / 64 GB 8 SATA + 2x M.2 Gen4 2x TB4, 2x 2.5GbE ~$4,308 (B&H) 
 Those prices are the enclosure only. Eight 18 TB drives, a 10 or 25 GbE card, and NVMe cache push a loaded TVS-h874T well past $6,000 before you have edited a single frame. That is the honest starting line. If you want the wider field of appliances at different price points, I compare them in the best storage appliances for creatives in 2026 .
 What Thunderbolt 4 delivers # 
 The marketing says Thunderbolt 4, and the port is 40 Gbps capable. The number that matters for editing is the one QNAP uses Thunderbolt networking to reach, and that caps at 20 Gbps per port. In ITPro's review, a 20 GB transfer over Thunderbolt hit about 1.3 GB/s, climbing to roughly 1.7 GB/s with SSDs in RAID (checked Jun 2026). That is comfortably past what a single 10GbE link gives you and plenty for multi-stream 4K, but it is not the headline 40 Gbps and it is not magic. The Thunderbolt port behaves like an IP link, not a raw block device, so you get a fast network share over a cable, not a directly attached volume.
 ~1.3 GB/s Real-world Thunderbolt transfer to the TVS-h874T in ITPro's test, rising to about 1.7 GB/s with RAID SSDs. The port is 40 Gbps rated; QNAP's Thunderbolt networking tops out at 20 Gbps (checked Jun 2026).
 The practical limit is that Thunderbolt serves one or two directly cabled seats. A four-person edit bay does not all plug into the same NAS, so the rest of the team rides the 2.5GbE ports or whatever 10/25 GbE card you add. That is what the two PCIe Gen 4 x16 slots are for: drop in a 10 or 25 GbE NIC and feed the networked seats, since 2x 2.5GbE on its own tops out around 600 MB/s aggregated and will bottleneck a room of editors pulling high-bitrate footage at once. The built-in GPU also hardware-accelerates transcoding, which is what makes proxy generation and quick client previews feel instant rather than queued. If your decision is direct-attach versus networked, that tradeoff deserves its own read: see Thunderbolt vs 10 GbE for editors .
 QuTS hero and the ZFS you are paying for # 
 The lowercase h in TVS-h874T means it runs QuTS hero, QNAP's ZFS operating system, rather than the ext4-based QTS. For a video library that is worth real money. ZFS checksums every block and self-heals silently corrupted data against a redundant copy, which is the protection against bit rot that ext4 does not have. QuTS hero adds copy-on-write, inline LZ4 compression (which helps on some RAW and intermediate files), inline deduplication, RAID-Z up to triple parity, and up to 65,536 snapshots per shared folder (checked Jun 2026 against QNAP's QuTS hero page). Snapshots are the part editors feel: a snapshot is a cheap, instant photo of the volume, so an overwritten project file or a bad render is a restore away.
 QuTS hero h6.0 went official on May 29, 2026, and added immutable snapshots that lock for a protection window so ransomware cannot alter or delete them, plus dual-NAS active-passive high availability, KMIP key management, and FIDO2 passkey logins. ZFS does have costs. It wants more RAM than ext4 (16 GB minimum for inline dedup, more recommended), and on QuTS hero you give up QTS features like Qtier auto-tiering. If you want ZFS explained without the QNAP framing, ZFS for video editors, explained plainly is the cleaner primer.
 The catch: the software surface # 
 A QNAP is not just a disk shelf. It is a small server running an app store: photo apps, media servers, a download manager, container station, surveillance, web apps. Every one of those is attack surface, and QNAP's history shows what that costs when one is exposed. The DeadBolt ransomware campaigns of 2022 and 2023 encrypted thousands of internet-facing QNAP devices, riding flaws like CVE-2022-27593 in the Photo Station app and CVE-2022-27596 affecting QTS and QuTS hero firmware (QNAP security advisories, summarized Jun 2026). The hardware was never the problem. The exposed services were.
 The mitigation is not exotic, but it is non-negotiable: do not port-forward the NAS to the open internet, disable the apps you do not use, keep firmware current, and reach it remotely through a private path rather than an open port. QNAP itself now leans on this with QuTS hero h6.0's immutable snapshots, which lock for a set window so even an attacker with admin cannot delete them inside that period, and with FIDO2 passkeys to kill password-stuffing. Those are real improvements, but they are seatbelts, not a reason to skip the lock on the front door. If your remote-editing plan involves opening the box up, read VPN vs mesh for remote editing first. A QNAP locked down to a LAN with snapshots and offsite backup is a solid, well-behaved box. A QNAP with its admin panel facing the internet is the cautionary tale. The richer the software surface, the more discipline it demands, and that is the real tradeoff against a barer appliance.
 Who QNAP is right for in 2026 # 
 Buy a Thunderbolt QNAP if you are a one-to-three-person studio that wants turnkey: a finished box with ZFS, a port you can plug a Mac straight into, a GPU for transcoding proxies, and a vendor's app ecosystem you will actually use. You are paying roughly $2,500 to $4,300 for the enclosure to skip the assembly and get a warranty, and for many shops that is the right call. The appliance roundup linked above puts QNAP next to its peers on price and posture.
 Be more skeptical if your value is mostly raw capacity per dollar, or if the app store makes you nervous and you would rather run a minimal, auditable stack. That is where a build-your-own NAS or a thinner platform competes, and where the mount layer matters more than the box. JuiceMount sits on top of storage you already own, turning a self-hosted NAS into a real Finder volume with local SSD cache and a local search index, at no per-seat cost. It pairs naturally with a QNAP you have locked down, and it is not the answer if what you want is QNAP's bundled apps doing the work for you. For the broader build question, build vs buy a NAS for a small post house walks the math.

 If your current NAS is not listed and Thunderbolt connectivity is essential, use the NAS Selector to narrow the options or browse and filter NAS Storage by ports and workload.
 The computer needs a Thunderbolt 3 or later port. A USB-C connector alone does not confirm Thunderbolt support because USB-C describes the connector rather than the communication protocol.
 Use a certified Thunderbolt 3, Thunderbolt 4, or Thunderbolt 5 cable. Intel specifies that certified Thunderbolt 4 cables can maintain 40Gbps capability at lengths up to two meters, so the cable does not need to be shorter than 0.8 meters. See Intel’s Thunderbolt 4 specifications .
 If you are unsure whether the computer or cable supports Thunderbolt, look for the Thunderbolt lightning symbol and check the computer manufacturer’s specifications.
 How Does a Thunderbolt NAS Connection Work?
 A UGREEN NAS remains a network storage system when connected through Thunderbolt:
 Computer → Thunderbolt network connection → Dedicated IP address → SMB or UGREEN NAS client → UGOS shared folder → NAS storage pool
 It does not give the computer direct control of the installed drives.
 UGOS  continues to manage the filesystem , storage pools, RAID , permissions, snapshots , and applications . The computer receives access to authorized shared folders through a high-speed network path.
 This is why a UGREEN NAS connected through Thunderbolt behaves differently from a Thunderbolt DAS enclosure. Our DAS-versus-NAS guide explains the architectural difference.
 How to Set Up a UGREEN NAS Thunderbolt Connection
 Before connecting the cable:
 Confirm that the NAS model appears in the supported table.
 Update UGOS to firmware 1.2.0.2121 or later.
 Confirm that the computer has a Thunderbolt 3, 4, or 5 port.
 Use a certified Thunderbolt cable instead of a standard USB-C charging cable.
 Create the storage pool and shared folder the computer will access.
 Keep the NAS connected to Ethernet if other devices still need LAN or remote access.
 Use the UGREEN NAS Download Center if you need the firmware or desktop client for your model.
 Connect the cable and find the Thunderbolt IP address
 Connect one end of the Thunderbolt cable to the supported UGREEN NAS.
 Connect the other end directly to the computer’s Thunderbolt port.
 Sign in to UGOS with an administrator account.
 Open Control Panel > Network Settings > Network Connection .
 Find the Thunderbolt network interface.
 Record its dedicated IP address, such as 172.17.70.242 .
 Open Control Panel > File Services > SMB .
 Enable SMB if it is not already active.
 Connect from Windows
 Open File Explorer.
 Select This PC .
 Open the three-dot menu and select Map network drive .
 Choose a drive letter.
 Enter the Thunderbolt IP address and shared-folder name:
` \\ 169.254.12.125\SharedFolder`
 Select **Reconnect at sign-in** if you want Windows to retain the mapping.
 Enter the NAS username and password.
 Open the mapped drive and transfer a test file.
 If the UGREEN NAS client is installed, you can also select More Connections and look for the device displaying the Thunderbolt symbol.
 Connect from macOS
 Open `System Settings > Network`.
 Confirm that **Thunderbolt Bridge** appears as a network service.
 If it is missing, add a network service and select Thunderbolt Bridge .
 Open Finder.
 Select `Go > Connect to Server`.
 Enter the Thunderbolt IP address and shared-folder name:
`smb://169.254.12.125/SharedFolder`
 Select Connect .
 Enter the NAS username and password.
 Choose the shared folder you want to mount.
 Apple identifies Thunderbolt Bridge as an IP network interface, and Finder accepts SMB addresses in the `smb://IP-address/share-name` format. See Apple’s instructions for Thunderbolt Bridge and connecting to an SMB server .
 You can also enable Bonjour under `Control Panel > File Services > Advanced Settings`, then look for the NAS under **Network** in Finder. Use the explicit Thunderbolt IP during initial testing so you know which connection the Mac is using.
 On supported models, the Thunderbolt connection can also provide a faster network path for the first full Time Machine backup than Wi-Fi. The backup destination and storage quota are still configured through SMB.
 How to Confirm the Transfer Is Using Thunderbolt
 Connecting the cable does not make an existing mapped share switch from Ethernet to Thunderbolt. A hostname can continue resolving to the NAS’s normal LAN address.
 Use the dedicated Thunderbolt IP for the first test:
 - Windows: `\169.254.x.x\SharedFolder`
- macOS: `smb://169.254.x.x/SharedFolder`
 Start a transfer using one large file of at least 20GB. Small files require more metadata and filesystem operations, making them unsuitable for measuring maximum sequential throughput.
 While the transfer is running:
 - On Windows, open Task Manager and check the Thunderbolt network adapter under Performance .
- On macOS, open Activity Monitor or Network settings and confirm activity on Thunderbolt Bridge.
- Check UGOS Task Manager for storage, network, processor, and memory activity.
- Repeat the transfer through the normal Ethernet address and compare the results.
 If the Thunderbolt adapter remains inactive, the computer is still using the LAN route. Remove the old mapping and reconnect using the explicit `169.254.x.x` address.
 Keep the default MTU while establishing this baseline. Jumbo frames require matching MTU support and configuration on both endpoints. Changing only one side can cause stalled or failed transfers.
 What Thunderbolt Transfer Speed Should You Expect?
 Thunderbolt 4 provides a 40Gbps link, but UGREEN direct connection carries IP and SMB traffic over that link. No single interface figure predicts the resulting file-transfer speed.
 The storage behind the connection frequently sets a lower ceiling:
 Component 
 Useful performance reference 
 Thunderbolt 4 interface 
 40Gbps link rate 
 NAS HDD 
 Approximately 200–260MB/s sequential 
 SATA SSD 
 Approximately 500–550MB/s 
 Four-drive HDD RAID 5 
 Approximately 600–700MB/s under favorable sequential conditions 
 NVMe storage pool 
 Can exceed 1GB/s when the client and protocol keep up 
 These storage figures are practical reference ranges, not guaranteed UGREEN NAS performance results.
 A DXP6800 Pro with an HDD RAID array will not transfer at the same speed as a DXP480T Plus with four fast NVMe SSDs. A faster connection cannot make the storage pool read or write beyond its own limit.
 {{UGPRODUCT}} 
 The client also matters. Copying data from the NAS to a laptop with a slower internal SSD stops at the laptop’s write speed. A high initial result followed by a sharp drop can mean that the client SSD has exhausted its write cache.
 Windows and macOS can produce different results because their network and SMB implementations differ. Compare each system against its own Ethernet baseline instead of assuming both platforms will reach the same speed.
 For sustained video work, calculate the required throughput from the number of streams and codec bitrate before deciding whether an HDD array or NVMe pool is sufficient. The UGREEN NAS video-editing guide provides the calculation and storage-performance references.
 Why Is the Thunderbolt Connection Slow or Unstable?
 Start with the symptom before changing RAID settings or buying hardware.
 Symptom 
 Likely cause 
 What to check first 
 No Thunderbolt interface appears 
 Unsupported model, old firmware, wrong cable, or USB-only computer port 
 Confirm the NAS model, firmware, computer port, and certified cable 
 Thunderbolt interface appears but the NAS will not open 
 SMB is disabled or the wrong address is being used 
 Enable SMB and connect using the Thunderbolt IP 
 Speed is unchanged from Ethernet 
 The mapped share still uses the LAN address 
 Remove it and map `169.254.x.x` directly 
 Network activity is high but file speed is low 
 NAS pool or client drive is limiting performance 
 Test the two storage paths separately 
 Large files are fast but small files are slow 
 Metadata and filesystem overhead 
 Test with one large file or archive small files before transfer 
 Transfer starts fast and then drops 
 SSD cache exhaustion or thermal throttling 
 Watch drive speed, written-data volume, and temperatures 
 Speed falls during a RAID rebuild or scrub 
 The storage pool is performing maintenance 
 Allow the maintenance task to finish 
 Connection fails after sleep 
 Computer power-management behavior 
 Review sleep, wake, and Thunderbolt power settings 
 Transfer starts and stalls after an MTU change 
 MTU mismatch 
 Restore the default MTU on both endpoints 
 Mac repeatedly connects and disconnects 
 Duplicate Thunderbolt Bridge services 
 Remove unused bridge services and reconnect 
 Windows desktop does not reconnect after sleep 
 BIOS or motherboard power setting 
 Review ErP Ready, Always On USB, and Thunderbolt Wake Support 
 The NAS is not detected
 Connect the NAS directly to the computer without a dock or adapter. If another Thunderbolt computer or cable is available, substitute one component at a time.
 Proving the physical link first is faster than changing SMB or storage settings before the NAS appears as a network interface.
 The share opens, but transfers are slow
 Confirm that the share uses the Thunderbolt IP, then test one large file in both directions.
 If the network interface reports substantially more throughput than the file copy, the network is not the primary bottleneck. Check:
 - Client read and write speed
- NAS storage-pool activity
- Installed drive performance
- RAID rebuilds and data scrubbing
- SMB signing or encryption
- Photo indexing and thumbnail generation
- Docker containers or virtual machines
- Cloud synchronization and backup tasks
 If the slowdown also occurs over Ethernet, continue with the broader UGREEN NAS performance troubleshooting guide .
 The transfer starts fast and then slows down
 A repeatable speed drop after a specific amount of data often points to write-cache exhaustion. Consumer SSDs can write quickly to a temporary cache and slow down after that cache fills.
 Heat creates a different pattern. During a sustained transfer, the NAS NVMe drives or the client SSD can reach a temperature that triggers thermal throttling. This is especially relevant to the all-NVMe DXP480T Plus.
 Watch drive temperatures while reproducing the slowdown. If performance returns after the drives cool, thermal throttling is likely. If the drop occurs after a similar amount of data during every test, cache exhaustion is the stronger explanation.
 The connection fails after sleep
 Sleep behavior depends on the computer and operating system.
 Some Windows laptops maintain the Thunderbolt connection in a low-power state. Some desktop systems cut power to the interface and do not reconnect it automatically. BIOS options such as ErP Ready , Always On USB , or Thunderbolt Wake Support can affect the result, although their names vary by motherboard.
 macOS deep sleep can disconnect Thunderbolt Bridge. If the connection does not return after wake:
 Open `System Settings > Network`.
 Confirm that Thunderbolt Bridge still appears.
 Remove duplicate Thunderbolt Bridge services.
 Disconnect and reconnect the cable.
 Reconnect the SMB share using the Thunderbolt IP.
 Do not disable operating-system security protections simply to preserve a storage connection during sleep.
 Other Thunderbolt devices reduce performance
 Several physical Thunderbolt ports on a computer can share the same controller and bandwidth. A dock, display, capture device, external SSD, or eGPU attached to that controller can compete with the NAS connection.
 Disconnect nonessential devices while testing. If the computer has ports connected to different Thunderbolt controllers, place the NAS and other high-bandwidth devices on separate controllers.
 Should You Use Thunderbolt or 10GbE?
 Thunderbolt and 10GbE solve different connection problems.
 Choose Thunderbolt direct connection when:
 One workstation needs a dedicated high-speed path.
 The computer and NAS are close enough for a direct cable.
 You want to avoid purchasing a 10GbE switch or computer adapter.
 The workstation regularly transfers large video, photo, or project files.
 Other devices can continue using the NAS through Ethernet.
 Choose 10GbE when:
 - Several computers need high-speed access.
- The NAS is located in another room.
- The connection must remain available when one workstation sleeps or disconnects.
- The studio already has a 10GbE switch and suitable cabling.
- You want every workstation to use the same network path.
 A supported UGREEN NAS can use both connections. Thunderbolt can provide a dedicated path to the primary workstation while Ethernet keeps the NAS available to other users and devices.
 Can You Connect an eGPU to UGREEN NAS?
 An eGPU attached to the computer is separate from the NAS. It can share the computer’s Thunderbolt-controller bandwidth with the NAS, so simultaneous GPU and storage activity can reduce transfer performance.
 Connecting an eGPU directly to the NAS is a different configuration. It requires support for the exact NAS model, GPU enclosure, graphics card, driver, and UGOS application. The Thunderbolt networking procedure in this article does not configure an external GPU.
 An eGPU connected to the NAS also does not become available inside Docker or a virtual machine through this setup. GPU passthrough for Docker and Virtual Machine is listed as a planned feature in the UGREEN System Update Plan .
 Use Thunderbolt direct connection for high-speed file access. Treat NAS-side GPU deployment as a separate workload with its own hardware and software requirements.
 Once the connection is working, test the explicit Thunderbolt IP with one large file. If the Thunderbolt adapter is active but file speed remains low, the storage path, client drive, or active workload is the next place to investigate.

 The Synology DS1525+ is the unit I keep coming back to when friends ask “what NAS should I actually buy?” It hits the sweet spot of five drive bays, real throughput for 4K editing, and an upgrade path to 10GbE without forcing you to spend enterprise money. When I had a two-editor project running over its 2.5GbE ports, we cut ProRes 422 HQ timelines without a single dropped frame. Add the optional E10G22-T1-Mini 10GbE adapter and you unlock 1,181 MB/s sequential throughput, which is genuinely faster than most spinning rust can sustain.
 For a film team of two to four editors, this is the right scale. Five bays give you enough capacity for a current project plus an archive, and you can add a Synology DX525 expansion unit later to push the system to 300TB. The DSM 7.3 update opened up third-party drive support, which is a real cost saver when you are filling five bays with IronWolf or Exos drives. Active media indexing, AI tagging, and Synology Photos keep your footage library searchable without paying for a separate DAM tool.
 Under the hood, you get an AMD Ryzen V1500B quad-core, 8GB of ECC-capable DDR4 (expandable to 32GB), and dual M.2 NVMe slots for read/write cache. For our team’s workload of mostly 4K H.264 with the occasional ProRes 422 job, the cache made a noticeable difference when scrubbing through long timelines. Plex and Jellyfin run smoothly on the same box if you want a media server side gig, though the V1500B is not a transcoding monster for heavy 4K HDR remuxing.
 The downsides are real but manageable. Some users report coil whine from the power supply on certain units, and Synology’s NVMe cache restriction still requires you to buy Synology-branded M.2 drives for the cache slots. Pricing is premium, but you are paying for Synology’s DSM software, which in my experience remains the most polished NAS operating system on the market. If you have a small post-production team and want a NAS that grows with you, the DS1525+ is the safest bet on this list.
 Compatibility with editing software
 The DS1525+ plays nicely with Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, and Final Cut Pro over SMB or iSCSI. We mapped it as a network drive in macOS and used Synology’s Drive ShareSync to keep proxies in sync with project files. Resolve’s collaborative workflow also works well when you point its database at the NAS, though I recommend keeping the live database on a local NVMe for performance and only moving finished renders to the NAS.
 If you cut on Windows, SMB MultiChannel support is the killer feature here. With two 2.5GbE ports aggregated, you can saturate the link for a single editor, and adding a 10GbE card turns the DS1525+ into a shared storage workhorse for a small team. Just make sure your switch and your workstation NIC support the same standard.
 Long-term reliability and warranty
 I have personally run a Synology NAS for over 6 years without a drive failure the unit did not handle, and other filmmakers I trust report 10+ years of trouble-free operation. The 3-year hardware warranty is solid, and Synology’s enterprise support tier (optional) is genuinely helpful if you are running mission-critical post workflows. For a working studio, that track record is worth the premium over cheaper brands.

I had the chance to stress-test one in a five-editor Resolve suite, and even with four streams of 4K ProRes 4444 playing back at the same time, the system did not stutter.
 The big upgrade over the older DS1821+ is the move to dual M.2 NVMe slots for caching and the option to install a 25GbE network card. For a studio working with 8K RAW or high-frame-rate 4K, that bandwidth matters. 25GbE is overkill for most teams, but it future-proofs your infrastructure for when you inevitably upgrade camera bodies. Standard 10GbE is still fully supported and is what I would actually wire up for a typical small studio.
 Synology’s DSM continues to lead the pack in usability, with snapshots, replication, active backup, and full virtualization support. If you want to run Docker containers for ffmpeg batch transcoding or render farm nodes, the DS1825+ will handle it. ECC memory support (with the right RAM) and high-availability clustering with a second unit make this a legitimate tier-1 storage solution for production companies who cannot afford downtime.
 There are some real concerns worth flagging. A number of users have reported high-pitched coil whine from the power supply on certain units, which is brutal in a quiet edit suite. The price is also a serious step up from the five-bay DS1525+, and as with all current Synology NVMe cache, you need Synology-branded M.2 drives. If your team is small (under five editors), I would point you to the DS1525+ instead. If you have a real post house with 8K projects and 10+ editors, this is the NAS to build around.
 Multi-editor performance in real workflows
 With dual 10GbE link aggregation, the DS1825+ handled five simultaneous 4K ProRes timelines in my test without any user feeling the network. The secret sauce is combining NVMe read cache with the 10GbE pipes. Without cache, even a fast 8-bay RAID 6 array can become the bottleneck when four editors are scrubbing through the same multicam project. With NVMe cache enabled, hot clips live in flash and the spinning drives handle the bulk storage.

The DS1825+ can sustain multiple streams of 8K BRAW with no proxy generation, which is rare for a NAS at this price tier. For VFX-heavy workflows where editors need to pull raw plates and rendered comps in parallel, this is one of the few NAS units that will not become the bottleneck.

If you are a solo editor or a two-person studio, the DS1825+ will leave 70% of its capacity and throughput sitting idle, and the price premium over a DS1525+ or UGREEN DXP6800 Pro is hard to justify. The eight-bay unit makes sense for established production companies, agencies with in-house post teams, and any shop that does long-format work (documentaries, series) where you are juggling multiple active projects at once.

 The Synology DS925+ is the NAS I recommend most often to filmmakers who are buying their first shared storage. It is small, quiet, and uses Synology’s famously polished DSM operating system. With four bays and dual 2.5GbE ports, it has enough capacity for a current project (around 60-80TB usable in RAID 5) and enough throughput for a single editor cutting 4K footage in Premiere Pro or Final Cut Pro without proxies.
 What I like most about the DS925+ is the software experience. If you have never set up a NAS before, DSM walks you through storage pools, user accounts, shared folders, and backup tasks in plain language. For filmmakers who are not IT pros, this matters more than raw benchmark numbers. The Synology Drive app gives you Dropbox-like syncing for project files, and Synology Photos handles stills and reference images. The 141-review average rating of 4.3 stars reflects how well-loved this unit is among home and small studio users.
 Performance from the AMD Ryzen V1500B platform is solid for a single user. Sequential reads and writes top out around 522/565 MB/s over the dual 2.5GbE ports in link aggregation. That is enough for one editor to scrub a 4K ProRes timeline without breaking a sweat. For two simultaneous editors, you will start to feel the limits unless you add a 10GbE NIC and configure SMB MultiChannel.
 The biggest issue right now is availability. At the time of writing, the DS925+ shows “only 1 left in stock” and is not Prime eligible, which makes it hard to recommend blindly. The NVMe cache slot restriction (Synology drives only) also remains a soft annoyance. If you can get one, it is a fantastic first NAS for a solo filmmaker or a small two-person studio. If stock is an issue, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus covers a similar role with faster 10GbE networking out of the box.
 Setting up the DS925+ for Premiere and Resolve
 The cleanest workflow I have tested is mapping the DS925+ as a network drive in macOS or Windows and pointing your NLE’s scratch disks at it. In Premiere Pro, set your media cache and project files to the NAS, and use the dedicated SSD cache for the project autosaves. In DaVinci Resolve, keep the live database on a local NVMe and only the source media on the NAS. Final Cut Pro users get the most benefit from macOS SMB optimization, but you may need to tweak Energy Saver settings to prevent the Mac from sleeping the network connection during long renders.
 For backup, use Synology Hyper Backup to mirror your project files to a USB drive, an offsite NAS, or Backblaze B2 cloud storage. The 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite) is the gold standard for protecting months of footage. The DS925+ makes it easy with built-in tools, and DSM’s snapshot feature lets you roll back accidental deletes or ransomware-style encryption without losing everything.
 Drive choices that match the DS925+

 How to Choose the Best NAS for Video Editing?
 Picking the right NAS for video editing is less about specs on a box and more about matching the unit to your specific codec, team size, and workflow. In this section, I will walk you through the four decisions that matter most: throughput sizing, networking, RAID configuration, and CPU/RAM. I have been through each of these decisions for my own projects, and the wrong call on any of them can mean dropped frames, sluggish scrubbing, or worse, lost footage.
 Step 1: Size your throughput for your codec
 Before you look at any NAS, you need to know how much bandwidth your footage actually needs. ProRes 422 HQ at 4K runs around 220 MB/s, ProRes 4444 at 4K hits 330 MB/s, and uncompressed 8K RAW can demand over 1,000 MB/s. H.264 and H.265 4K footage typically runs 50-150 MB/s depending on bit depth and frame rate. A single editor cutting compressed 4K can get by on 1GbE (115 MB/s), but a single editor cutting ProRes 4K needs 2.5GbE at minimum, and multi-editor workflows need 10GbE.
 As a rule of thumb, multiply your codec’s bitrate by 1.5x to leave headroom for playback, then multiply by the number of simultaneous editors. That number is your minimum network bandwidth. If you are running 2.5GbE NAS, you are limited to about 280 MB/s, which is fine for one ProRes 422 HQ editor. If you have two or more editors on ProRes or 8K footage, you need 10GbE.
 Step 2: Choose between 2.5GbE, 10GbE, and Thunderbolt
 2.5GbE is the new baseline for video editing NAS in 2026. It is fast enough for single-editor ProRes 422 workflows, affordable (cables and switches are cheap), and supported by most modern motherboards without an extra NIC. 10GbE is what you want for team workflows or for cutting ProRes 4444 / 8K footage. A basic 10GbE switch and a single 10GbE NIC for your editing workstation costs a few hundred dollars and is well worth the investment for any serious post setup.
 Thunderbolt is a different beast. It is a direct-attached protocol that does not need a switch, hits 20-40Gbps in real-world use, and feels like a local NVMe drive to the operating system. For solo Mac editors, Thunderbolt-based NAS like the QNAP TBS-h574TX or UGREEN DXP6800 Pro can be a sweet spot. The catch is that Thunderbolt does not work well for multi-user scenarios, so plan to add 10GbE for any team setup.
 Step 3: Pick the right RAID level
 RAID is not a backup, but it is a critical safety net. For video editing NAS, you have three main options. RAID 5 gives you one-drive fault tolerance with the best capacity (N-1 drives worth of usable space), and is appropriate for 3-5 bay units. RAID 6 gives you two-drive fault tolerance, which is worth the capacity trade-off for 6+ bay units holding months of footage. RAID 10 stripes and mirrors for maximum performance, but you lose half your capacity, so it only makes sense for high-performance scratch volumes.
 For a solo editor with 4-5 bays, RAID 5 is fine. For a small team with 6+ bays, RAID 6 is the safer pick. For a portable all-flash unit, RAID 0 (no redundancy) is acceptable because you should never store your only copy on a portable drive anyway. Always pair RAID with an offsite backup (the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite) using Backblaze B2, Amazon S3 Glacier, or a second NAS at a different physical location.
 Step 4: Match CPU and RAM to your workload
 The CPU in your NAS handles file transfers, RAID calculations, snapshots, encryption, and any apps you run (Plex, Docker, virtual machines). For a simple storage-only NAS, an ARM or entry-level x86 chip is fine. For a NAS that also runs Plex transcoding, virtual machines, or a render farm, you want a real Intel i5 or AMD Ryzen with at least 4 cores. The units on this list range from ARM-based Synology units to 10-core Intel i5 systems, and the right pick depends on whether you are using the NAS purely for storage or as a multi-purpose server.
 RAM matters more than most buyers realize. 8GB is the minimum for a video editing NAS in 2026. 16GB is comfortable for multi-user workflows plus Docker apps. 32GB is appropriate for 8K editing, large-scale transcoding, or running multiple virtual machines. ECC memory (in units like the Asustor Lockerstor 10 Gen3 and UGREEN DXP4800 GT) is a server-grade feature that prevents silent data corruption, which is a meaningful safety net for irreplaceable footage.
 Step 5: Budget tier recommendations for filmmakers
 Under $600 is the budget tier. The UGREEN DXP4800 GT and DXP4800 Plus fit here, and they are excellent for solo editors cutting 4K H.264/H.265 or single-editor ProRes workflows. Pair one with 4x 12TB IronWolf drives and a single 2TB NVMe for cache, and you have a complete editing NAS for under $1,500 all-in.
 $600-$1,200 is the sweet spot for most small studios. The Synology DS1525+, Synology DS1825+, and UGREEN DXP6800 Pro live here, and they support multi-editor workflows, 10GbE, and substantial capacity. This is the tier I recommend for most post-production setups.
 $1,200+ is the professional tier. The Synology DS1825+ with expansion units, the Asustor Lockerstor 10 Gen3, and the QNAP TBS-h574TX belong here. These are the units you buy when you have 5+ editors, 100TB+ of active footage, or specific workflow requirements like Thunderbolt 4 or all-flash performance.
 Don’t forget power protection
 One thing most NAS buying guides skip is the UPS. A sudden power loss during a write to a spinning drive can corrupt files, and a sudden loss during a RAID rebuild can be catastrophic. A basic uninterruptible power supply (UPS) like the APC Back-UPS Pro 1500 or CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD costs around $200-300 and plugs into your NAS via USB. The NAS monitors the UPS and shuts down gracefully when battery is low. This single $200 purchase can save you from losing a project. I learned this the hard way after a brownout ate a 4TB external drive in 2018, and I have not run a NAS without a UPS since.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is a NAS good for video editing?
 Yes, a NAS is excellent for video editing. It provides centralized storage accessible by multiple editors over your network, offers data redundancy through RAID configurations, and modern 10GbE NAS units can sustain the high throughput required for real-time 4K and 8K video editing without proxies. Solo editors benefit from having a single source of truth for footage, while teams benefit from simultaneous multi-user access to the same project files.
 Which NAS is best for video editing?
 The best NAS for video editing depends on your team size and codec. For solo editors, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus or Synology DS925+ are excellent. For small teams (2-5 editors) cutting 4K ProRes, the Synology DS1525+ or UGREEN DXP6800 Pro are the best value. For professional studios with 8K workflows or 5+ editors, the Synology DS1825+ or Asustor Lockerstor 10 Gen3 are the top picks.
 Is 32GB RAM overkill for video editing?
 For a solo editor working with 4K footage, 8-16GB of RAM in your NAS is sufficient. However, 32GB becomes necessary when multiple users simultaneously access the NAS, when running additional services like Plex or virtual machines, or when working with 8K and multi-cam projects where the NAS CPU benefits from more memory for file handling and cache operations.
 Which NAS is the best for backup?
 Any NAS with RAID 5 or RAID 6 configuration serves as an excellent backup destination. For a backup-focused NAS, look for models with strong backup software (Synology Hyper Backup, QNAP HBS3, or UGREEN’s built-in tools), cloud sync integration, and at least 4 drive bays to run RAID 5 or 6 for redundancy. The Synology DS1525+ and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are both excellent choices for dedicated backup workflows.
 Do I need 10GbE for video editing NAS?
 10GbE is recommended for any multi-editor workflow or for solo editors cutting ProRes 422 HQ or higher bitrate codecs. For a single editor cutting compressed 4K H.264 or H.265, 2.5GbE may be sufficient. As a guideline, if your footage bitrate exceeds 200 MB/s or you have two or more editors, you need 10GbE.
 What RAID level is best for video editing NAS?
 RAID 5 is the standard choice for 4-5 bay NAS units, providing one-drive fault tolerance with the best capacity. RAID 6 is recommended for 6+ bay units, providing two-drive fault tolerance for added safety with larger capacity arrays. RAID 10 is appropriate for high-performance scratch volumes where speed matters more than capacity. Always pair RAID with an offsite backup for true data protection.
 Final Verdict: Which NAS Should You Buy?
 After weeks of testing and dozens of conversations with working editors, here is how I would actually spend your money on the best NAS for video editing and backup. If you are a solo filmmaker or one-person studio, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus hits the sweet spot of price, performance, and reliability. Its dual 10GbE ports, 144TB capacity ceiling, and 4.6-star rating from over 600 owners make it the safest default pick in 2026.
 For a small team of 2-4 editors, the Synology DS1525+ remains the most reliable choice. You pay a premium over UGREEN, but you get the most mature NAS software on the market, enterprise-grade support, and a track record of 5+ years of firmware updates. If your team is 5+ editors or you are cutting 8K footage, the Synology DS1825+ or the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro are the units to consider. Both offer dual 10GbE, scalable capacity, and the headroom to grow with your studio.
 Whatever you choose, do not forget the basics. Pair your NAS with NAS-rated drives (IronWolf, IronWolf Pro, WD Red Pro), put it on a UPS to protect against power loss, and set up a real 3-2-1 backup strategy with an offsite copy. Storage fails quietly and without warning, and the only thing standing between you and a lost project is the redundancy you built before you needed it. Now go clear some footage.

 Reasons to avoid

 Buy it if:
 ✅ Setting up tech usually frustrates you: Setup is genuinely tool-free and can be completed in under 10 minutes, so even first-time NAS users can get started without hassle.
 ✅ Keeping files safe is your priority: RAID and hot-swap drive support deliver straightforward backup and recovery, making the F2-425 a safe choice for storing important files.
 ✅ You like peace and quiet: During testing, the F2-425 was barely audible even under load, so it won't disrupt your work or living space.
 Don't buy it if:
 ❌ Future network growth is your priority: With only a single 2.5GbE port, the F2-425 limits high-speed connections and network expansion options.
 ❌ Business-class multitasking is a must for you: If you want business-class features or heavy multitasking, a larger model like the F4-424 Pro is a better fit than the simpler, more affordable F2-425.
 The TerraMaster F2-425 stands out for its genuinely tool-free, under-10-minute setup, making it one of the most accessible NAS options for beginners. We found that getting started required no special skills or extra hardware, so you can go from unboxing to storing files in minutes.
 On the practical side, the F2-425 supports RAID and hot-swap drives, which means you get automatic data protection and simple recovery options if a drive fails. This sort of reliability is especially reassuring if you’re using the NAS for backups or as your main storage hub. No need for advanced IT knowledge.
 Compared to the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro , the F2-425 is a more straightforward, affordable choice. It doesn't offer the same room for business-class expansion or heavy multitasking, but for personal use or a small office, the simplicity and lower price make a lot more sense if you don’t need top-tier specs.
 That said, the F2-425 does only offer a single 2.5GbE network port, which limits your options if you’re planning to upgrade your network or need faster, multi-user transfers. If connectivity is your top concern, you’ll want to keep this in mind when weighing alternatives.
 Where the F2-425 really shines is in day-to-day use: during testing, it ran exceptionally quiet, barely audible in a home office, even under load. If you want a low-maintenance NAS that blends into your workspace and doesn’t become a distraction, this is a practical, set-and-forget solution for creative users or first-time NAS buyers.

 Best NAS device: Frequently asked questions 
 What is a NAS device?
 Network-attached storage devices connect your data to your local network and the internet, with the added benefit of being accessible locally. They typically store data in an array of drives, either used purely for storage or with one or more drives dedicated to parity - ensuring that data can be reconstituted in event of a drive failure.
 You buy your server, either part-by-part to build it yourself, or pre-built from a manufacturer, your drives (should yours not already have one or more included, or you’re wanting to upgrade or replace them), and quite possibly your chosen NAS distribution, such as OpenMediaVault or Unraid.
 Plus, a NAS distribution is almost guaranteed to come pre-installed, albeit quite possibly a proprietary one that, though intuitive, may give you less control under the hood. If you’re only clear on what a NAS device does instead of how one works, however, this could be a selling point.
 Can I use my existing drives with a NAS device?
 Almost certainly yes. Though they’re near-enough always fitted with internal drives, even the best pre-built NAS devices are designed such that you can connect and mount your portable storage to a NAS server too. In that sense, a NAS device doesn’t have to replace your existing storage solutions or backups, but can absolutely compliment them.
 Barring NAS manufacturers that get picky over which third party drives they support (the QNAP TVS-h674T, which we like for its sheer amount of drive bays, falls foul of this), this also applies to the internal drives you already have - providing the filesystem is in the right format for your new device.
 Why are NAS devices important for businesses?
 In the age of remote and hybrid work, NAS devices are a way of giving employees high-speed access to files out of the office while also allowing a business to maintain control over those files because they’re held locally, as opposed to on a cloud storage service which may or may not have end-to-end encryption. 
 A dedicated parity drive can reconstruct your data in the event of a drive failure without reliance on ‘Big Tech’ infrastructure.
 NAS devices also make ideal office servers for solo professionals and small studios who would benefit from local processing power, such as photo and video editing outfits who need lightning, often simultaneous uploads on the fly as they export incremental edits to files in a project.
 The upshot of choosing a NAS device over a cloud storage service is that, minus your ongoing electricity bill, the costs involved are one-offs instead of a running subscription. Mind you, many of our choices are also power efficient, so you don’t need to associate these hulking monoliths with high power consumption.
 How do you choose a NAS device?
 If it’s pure data storage capacity that you’re after, consider the number of bays. If it’s network performance, consider the standard of ethernet port (some are 10GbE, whilst some are 2.5GbE which will affect some high-speed environments), as well as the availability of Thunderbolt on the device.
 Sometimes it just depends on how big and loud the device is, and whether that works for you. Some of our best choices pack a punch, but are also hard to conceal in quiet or cramped environments. Others, meanwhile, are concealable and quiet, with concessions instead made to performance.

 Troubleshooting a slow editing NAS
 10GbE NAS performs poorly
 Verify that the client actually negotiated 10GbE; a 1GbE or 2.5GbE adapter caps the path.
 Check switch ports, cabling and adapters.
 Look for RAID rebuilds, near-full volumes, indexing, antivirus scans, SMB signing/encryption overhead and saturated CPU or memory.
 Test large sequential files separately from many-small-file workloads.
 Benchmarks are fast but playback stutters
 Sequential benchmarks may not represent NLE metadata access. Stuttering can come from H.265/RAW decoding, effects, cache stored on the NAS, competing users, packet loss, unsuitable project databases or a RAID layout with poor write behavior.
 Mac cannot mount or reliably use a share
 Use current SMB rather than legacy AFP, confirm user permissions and firmware, avoid problematic share names, check signing/encryption settings and ensure the Mac is wired rather than on Wi-Fi. For Thunderbolt networking, verify supported macOS versions, drivers, cables and topology.

 Editing from different locations? Prioritize proxies, synchronization and application collaboration over NAS bandwidth alone.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is 10GbE necessary for editing video from a NAS?
 It is the sensible baseline for serious direct 4K editing and many solo 6K/8K workflows. A 2.5GbE system can suit one editor using moderate-bitrate media and local cache; 25GbE is preferable for all-flash, multicam, high-bitrate 8K and multiple editors.
 Can a NAS edit 8K video without proxies?
 Sometimes, on a properly configured local 10GbE or 25GbE network with fast storage and suitable codecs. 8K RAW, multicam and complex effects may still require proxies because workstation decoding and processing, not storage delivery, becomes the limit.
 Is RAID a backup for video projects?
 No. RAID helps maintain availability after certain drive failures but does not protect against deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, corruption or NAS failure. Keep an independent backup and an off-site or offline copy.
